Effective co-training strategy mitigates catastrophic forgetting while preserving upstream performance (<2% degradation on Matbench Discovery)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Nequix, MACE-MP-0, OAM), benchmarks, and property types (2nd/3rd order force constants, thermal conductivity)
Strong empirical results: 55% average improvement on phonon properties, state-of-the-art among MPtrj-trained models, with consistent gains across base models

weaknesses: Critical scope limitation: All evaluations restricted to equilibrium configurations only. This severely limits applicability to production MLIPs that must handle highly distorted non-equilibrium geometries. MD stability check (A.6) is insufficient (only 5 systems, 100 ps)

Data leakage concerns: 99% of MDR Phonon materials exist in MPtrj pretraining set. Fine-tuning on same materials (just at displaced positions) is not true out-of-distribution evaluation. Claims of generalization are overstated

Energy dataset mismatch (Section A.2): 31.60 meV/atom MAE between PBE MDR and MPtrj with outliers to 1.5 eV/atom indicates incompatible training/fine-tuning data. The ~30 meV/atom error floor is concerning

Limited technical novelty: Combines existing ideas incrementally. Hessian training done by Fang et al. (2024) and Gangan et al. (2025); HVP scalability used by Amin et al. (2025); co-training is standard. Stochastic column sampling is moderately novel but straightforward

Incomplete evaluation on non-phonon tasks: Matbench Discovery (Table 4) shows no improvements on geometry optimization. Elastic properties (Table A.3) show mixed results. No evaluation on thermal expansion or off-equilibrium properties

Hyperparameter sensitivity without principled guidance: λ_Φ sensitivity (A.4) shows substantial variation; even higher λ_Φ achieves better phonon metrics. Choice of λ_Φ=100 appears arbitrary. No method provided for selecting hyperparameters for new datasets

Theoretical justification is informal: Why stochastic HVP works as well as full Hessian is justified only 'in expectation' without convergence analysis. Connection between Hessian error and phonon errors is empirical but not theoretically justified
Unexplained design choices: λ_E = 0 during PFT means energy is not supervised; rationale not provided. Why does fine-tuning directly on phonon displacements fail (Fig. 3, Table 1)? No analysis given
Generalization across functionals not explored: All experiments use PBE only. Unclear if PFT transfers to LDA, hybrid functionals, or other DFT variants, limiting broader applicability

Third-order improvements less compelling: 20-30% improvement on third-order force constants is substantially smaller than 55% for second-order, suggesting benefits don't transfer uniformly to higher derivatives

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Strong empirical demonstration (Figure 2) that Hessian error correlates with phonon property errors, providing solid justification for direct curvature supervision.

Clever and practical scaling technique: Stochastic Hessian-vector product (HVP) reduces computational complexity from O(N²) to O(N), enabling training on realistic large supercells with ~30× speedup while maintaining comparable accuracy (Appendix A.1).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple base models tested, diverse metrics (phonon frequencies, entropy, free energy, heat capacity), generalization to third-order properties, extensive ablations and hyperparameter analysis in appendices.

Strong empirical results: 55% average improvement on phonon properties, state-of-the-art performance for MPtrj-trained models, consistent benefits across different architectures (Nequix, MACE) and larger upstream datasets (OAM).
Good reproducibility practices: Code and data promised, detailed hyperparameters provided, implementation details in appendices, clear method description enabling reproduction.
Practical co-training solution: Simple batch alternation strategy effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting with <1% degradation on Matbench Discovery stability task.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Training MLIPs on Hessians is not new; concurrent work exists (Fang et al. 2024, Gangan et al. 2025, Amin et al. 2025, Burger et al. 2025). Main contribution—stochastic HVP—is an incremental engineering optimization. Co-training is simple batch alternation.

Narrow and primarily equilibrium-scoped evaluation: Explicitly restricted to materials at or near equilibrium; no off-equilibrium testing, no molecular dynamics at finite temperature, no defect calculations. Severely limits applicability of MLIPs to real-world use cases.

Critical unexplained anomaly: Fine-tuning directly on phonon displacement DFT data dramatically worsens Hessian error (182 K vs base 24 K, Table 1), despite displacement data containing direct Hessian information. This fundamental question receives no satisfactory explanation, undermining understanding of why the method works.

Unresolved dataset mismatch: Section A.2 documents 31.60 meV/atom systematic energy shift between MPtrj and MDR Phonon with outliers to 1.5 eV/atom. Acknowledged ~30 meV/atom energy floor suggests results may be systematically biased and evaluation metrics less clean than presented.

Fundamental tension masked by co-training: Necessity of K=4 co-training ratio reveals Hessian and EFS objectives are partially at odds. Without co-training, Hessian supervision causes >5% RMSD and >60% F1 degradation on stability classification. This is addressed via ad-hoc patching rather than principled objective design.

Missing critical comparisons: No direct comparison with Fang et al. (2024) which also uses analytical Hessians for phonons; no baseline of training from scratch on phonon data; limited comparison with concurrent cited methods. Difficult to assess relative merit.

Evaluation contamination: Test materials overlap with base model training data (MPtrj and MDR Phonon share ~9,868 materials). While phonon calculations are new, materials themselves were in upstream training, limiting generalization claims.

Hyperparameter selection under-explored: Appendix A.4 shows λΦ = 1000 achieves better phonon metrics (10/9/3/2 K) than chosen λΦ = 100 (12/14/5/3 K), yet selection criterion is vague ('maintain phonon performance without degradation'). No principled framework for balancing competing objectives.

Overstated computational efficiency claims: Paper states '1% of original pretraining cost' but actually uses 35 A100 hours (35% of 100-hour Nequix MP training). HVP incurs 3× time/memory overhead (Appendix A.7). '1%' claim is misleading.

Shallow analysis of generalization: No per-material analysis of which chemistries/structures benefit most. Third-order force constant improvements (20-30%) smaller than second-order (55%), yet attribution unclear since thermal conductivity depends on both Φ² and Φ³. Transfer to new materials not demonstrated.

strengths: Strong empirical results: 55% average error reduction on phonon properties, achieving state-of-the-art for MPtrj-trained models
Scalable methodology: Stochastic Hessian-vector product efficiently reduces complexity from O(N²) to O(N), enabling training on large supercells
Practical utility: Uses data already generated in standard DFT workflows; only 35 A100 hours training cost

Thorough experimental evaluation: Comprehensive ablations demonstrating necessity of each component, tests across multiple base models (Nequix, MACE), and unexpected finding that direct displacement training fails badly
Generalization: Improvements extend to third-order force constants (20-30% reduction) and thermal conductivity (31% improvement) without explicit training
Reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters provided, code/models/data release promised, clear ablation studies enable reproduction
Model-agnostic: Demonstrated effectiveness across different architectures, not limited to single model type
Honest limitations discussion: Out-of-equilibrium configurations, non-equivariant architecture constraints, and dataset mismatch issues acknowledged
weaknesses: Energy mismatch between datasets (31.60 meV/atom between MDR Phonon and MPtrj) inadequately addressed; relegated to appendix despite potentially affecting results and requiring zero force/stress assumptions

Limited theoretical understanding: Why direct displacement training fails dramatically is observed but not explained; receptive field argument (Sec 3.5) insufficiently developed; stochastic sampling convergence analysis absent

Generalization uncertainty: All experiments use Materials Project data with ~99% overlap between MPtrj and MDR Phonon; OAM training includes MPtrj, limiting independence; no testing on structurally different datasets

Specialized impact: Results primarily benefit phonon predictions; Matbench Discovery stability shows negligible improvements; elastic properties mixed (bulk modulus worsens), limiting claim of general MLIP improvement
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices: Co-training ratio K=4 based on GPU budget rather than principled tuning; test set construction rationale unclear; learning rate selection lacks specificity
Limited comparison with related work: Recent Hessian-based approaches (Fang et al. 2024, Amin et al. 2025) mentioned but not compared empirically; distinction from prior art could be clearer
Column sampling justification: While Appendix A.1 shows empirical speedup, theoretical analysis of uniform random sampling optimality relative to symmetry-aware alternatives is absent

Incomplete analysis: Failure modes not discussed; minimum phonon data requirements unclear; quantitative comparison between analytical and finite displacement methods mentioned as 'near identical' but specifics missing
